rows.verified: There is no universal legal maximum workplace temperature because workplaces and heat-generating processes differ.
Employers must comply with health and safety law, including maintaining a comfortable temperature and clean, fresh air.
Indoor workplaces should normally be at least 16°C, or 13°C where much of the work involves rigorous physical effort.
Temperature controls should reflect whether work is indoors or outdoors and the environment's normal operating temperature.
Local heating or cooling can be used where a comfortable temperature cannot be maintained throughout a workroom.
Heat stress depends on more than air temperature, including work rate, humidity, air movement, heat sources and work clothing.
Dehydration in very hot conditions can seriously affect health and the ability to work safely.
For high work rates in heat-stress conditions, HSE guidance indicates workers may need around 250 ml of fluid every 15 minutes.
Thermal risk depends on air temperature, radiant heat, humidity, airflow, clothing, metabolic workload, hydration and acclimatisation.
HSE temperature evidence is workplace-, weather-, task-, worker-, clothing-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level heat-illness probability.
LOLER places duties on people and organisations that own, operate or control lifting equipment.
Most lifting equipment is also work equipment, so PUWER inspection and maintenance requirements commonly apply.
Lifting operations must be properly planned by a competent person.
Lifting operations must be appropriately supervised and carried out safely.
Lifting equipment must be fit for purpose, appropriate for the task, suitably marked and of adequate strength and stability.
Many lifting systems require periodic thorough examination, with records retained and dangerous defects reported.
Lifting equipment includes work equipment for lifting or lowering loads and accessories used to support, fix or anchor it.
Equipment used to lift people must generally be thoroughly examined every six months or according to an examination scheme.
Lifting risk depends on load, equipment, accessories, configuration, ground, environment, operator competence, planning and supervision.
HSE LOLER evidence is lift-, load-, equipment-, operator-, site-, examination- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level lifting-incident probability.
PUWER requires work equipment to be suitable for its intended use.
Work equipment must be safe, maintained in a safe condition and inspected where installation or deterioration can affect safety.
Equipment may be used only by people who have received adequate information, instruction and training.
Protective measures normally include guarding, emergency stops, energy isolation, visible markings and warning devices.
Equipment must be maintained in an efficient state, efficient order and good repair, with maintenance logs kept current where used.
